# The phenomenon of inversion 

As I’ve gotten older I’ve noticed a curious thing:

- Nonprofit, public service “do gooder” types can be quite into their personal goals and objectives. A first order description of those fields is people who do things for others. Yet most of the people I meet that work in those fields are very into what they’d like to see changed in the world, their work life balance, stuff like that. 
- Private sector, business “money focused” type are often focused on meeting others goals and objectives. The first order description of those fields is people who do things to make money for themselves. Yet most of the people I meet who work in those fields are focused on others, either through customer service or making money to support a family, help friends etc. 

This relates to Jane Jacob’s distinction between guardian and trader ethics, a concept I am grateful to VGR for introducing me to: 

[Jacobs lays this out in *Systems of Survival*, a dialogue about the two basic ways people earn a living and the moral codes that go with each. She argues that there are two "moral syndromes," meaning clusters of values that tend to travel together, and that each one evolved to suit a distinct kind of work.

The **guardian syndrome** belongs to those whose work is to protect, to take, or to hold territory: government, the military, the police, the clergy, aristocracies, and (by extension) much of what we now call public service. Its precepts include shunning trade, exerting prowess, being obedient and disciplined, adhering to tradition, respecting hierarchy, being loyal, taking vengeance, deceiving for the sake of the task, making rich use of leisure, being ostentatious, dispensing largesse, and being honorable. Guardians value loyalty, honor, and fidelity to a mission larger than themselves.

The **trader syndrome** belongs to those whose work is to exchange goods and services: commerce, industry, science, and the professions that serve a market. Its precepts include shunning force, coming to voluntary agreements, being honest, collaborating easily with strangers and aliens, competing, respecting contracts, using initiative and enterprise, being open to inventiveness and novelty, being efficient, promoting comfort and convenience, dissenting for the sake of the task, investing for productive purposes, being industrious, being thrifty, and being optimistic. Traders value honesty, openness, and the ability to deal with anyone.

Jacobs's central claim is that both codes are legitimate and necessary, and that trouble comes when they are mixed. She calls the result a "monstrous hybrid." When guardians take on trader activities, you get corruption, patronage, and the mafia, or a state that runs businesses to enrich its officials. When traders take on guardian values, you get things like cartels, monopolies enforced by coercion, and guilds that use force or secrecy to protect their turf. Each code works because it fits its own task. Honesty and voluntary agreement make trade function, while loyalty and discipline make protection function.

This is what makes the pattern I've noticed so interesting. In my experience, the people in guardian-coded fields often behave with more trader-like, individualistic sensibilities, while those in trader-coded fields often display the guardian virtues of loyalty, service, and obligation to others. The stated ethic of the field and the lived ethic of its people seem to have swapped places.]

***

### Regarding the title: 

[I chose the word "inversion" with Marx in mind, specifically *The German Ideology*, which he wrote with Engels in the mid-1840s. The manuscript is aimed at the Young Hegelians, who believed that ideas drive history: change how people think and you change the world. Marx's reply is that this has the relationship backwards. "Life is not determined by consciousness, but consciousness by life." People's ideas about themselves come out of the material conditions in which they live and work, not the other way around.

The image he uses is the camera obscura. In one, the world appears upside down on the back wall, and Marx says ideology works the same way: "men and their circumstances appear upside-down." He doesn't mean people are stupid or lying. The inversion arises from their actual life-process, just as the flipped image on the retina arises from the physics of the eye. The distortion comes with the position you occupy, and the story people tell about what they're doing and why can run opposite to what the structure of their work makes them do. A related point is that the dominant ideas of an age tend to be those that serve the people in power, who present their particular interests as the common good.

Here is how I'm using this. Marx wasn't writing about nonprofits and businesses, and I don't want to pretend he was. But the shape of the argument fits what I've been noticing. The *stated* ethic of a field is its ideology, the story it tells about itself: this work is for others, or this work is for profit. The *lived* ethic comes from the material situation of the people inside it. Someone in a mission-driven job still has to build a career, protect their time, and make a life, and the language of the mission gives those personal projects a respectable vocabulary. Someone in a commercial job depends on customers, colleagues, and a family they're supporting, so their daily reality is one of obligation to others, whatever the field says about self-interest.

Read this way, the inversion isn't hypocrisy. The label on the field is the upside-down image, and the behavior of the people in it is closer to the thing itself. That is also why I think Jacobs and Marx fit together here. Jacobs gives the two codes, and Marx suggests why the codes people profess can drift away from the ones they practice.
